note: A careful rendering of a difficult customs-evasion passage; the obscure lines on miraculous power and mantras are rendered literally and defensibly.

errors.why: ནམ་སྲོས is dusk/nightfall: Udāyin had not come back by nightfall (he arrives after dark on the next side), not that he stayed out until dawn.

fix.replace: had still not come by nightfall

errors.english: Heavy materials used for plastering [note: such as dung] should be set on a stone.
errors.why: ལྕི་བ here is cow dung (the material for plaster), not 'heavy'; the dung is to be put on a potsherd.

note: Sound Vinaya prose with correct technical vocabulary; one time-of-day error and a misread ལྕི་བ.

errors.english: Not understanding the opponent's thought, one might formulate an objection beginning with
errors.why: གཞན་གྱིས is the agent: another party (the opponent), not understanding the intended meaning, says 'the external ones…'; it is not someone misunderstanding the opponent.

fix.find: Not understanding the opponent's thought, one might formulate an objection
fix.replace: Not understanding the intended meaning, someone else (an opponent) states the objection

errors.english: Through the force of excessive conceptual attachment
errors.why: ལྷག་པར་ཞེན་པ is adhyavasāya, conceptual determination, a technical epistemological term, not 'excessive attachment'.

errors.english: That is to say, does it engage with specific characteristics?
errors.why: The gloss only identifies 'those' as the svalakṣaṇas: the question is whether conceptual thought does NOT operate on them; the English turns it into the opposite question.

note: Generally faithful apoha discussion, but the opponent's objection is misattributed and adhyavasāya is mistranslated.

errors.english: If words were to engage strictly with the ultimate truth, then the words for the objects of other philosophical views would not engage without a cause.
errors.why: These are the summary verses (named as such right after) and are turned into prose; and རྒྱུ་མེད་ཅན qualifies the objects of other views as baseless, it does not mean words 'would not engage without a cause'.

fix.find: If words were to engage strictly with the ultimate truth, then the words for the objects of other philosophical views would not engage without a cause. Furthermore, regarding the past and the unborn, no words would ever have a false object. Therefore, these are held to be the objects of the mind.
fix.replace:
If [words] engaged solely with the ultimate,
words would not apply to the baseless objects
of other particular views;
and since no word about the past or the unborn
would have a false object,
these are held to have the mind's object as their domain.

errors.english: This is because it is not the actual reality as it is perceived
errors.why: མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ is conceptual determination (adhyavasāya), not perception; the point is that reality is not as it is conceptually construed, which matters in Dharmakīrti.

note: Usable outline of the argument, but the summary verses are prosified and garbled and key epistemic terms are flattened.

errors.english: there are diverse possessors of blue and so forth
errors.why: ལྡན་པ here is the Vaiśeṣika quality saṃyoga, a variegated conjunction of blue etc., not 'possessors'; the 'possession' rendering throughout obscures the category.

errors.english: because inherence converges in a single possessed object
errors.why: The Tibetan says the conjunction inheres (samavāya) in a single object; the English makes 'inherence' the subject and the object 'possessed'.

note: Follows the anti-Vaiśeṣika argument correctly overall; the rendering of saṃyoga as 'possession' makes some sentences hard to follow.

errors.english: Is it not unreasonable to say, སྐྱེས་མོས་ཀྱིས
errors.why: The Tibetan word (probably corrupt) is left untranslated inside the English sentence rather than being rendered or flagged in a note.

errors.english: The bare nature devoid of that, a cognition following upon perception, is conceived as what produces its own aspect.
errors.why: The bare nature is known by the cognition that follows perception, and that cognition conceives it as the producer of its own aspect; the English equates the nature with the cognition.

note: A faithful reading of the dream and non-deception passage; only the last argument about absence is a little blurred.

errors.english: since making the pervaded understood is fitting for making the qualifier understood
errors.why: The roles are swapped: the qualified (= the pervaded, the reason) is fit to make the pervader (the probandum) understood.

fix.find: since making the pervaded understood is fitting for making the qualifier understood
fix.replace: since the qualified (the pervaded) is fit to be what makes the pervader understood

errors.english: a part of that subject quality
errors.why: This is the root phrase pakṣadharmas tadaṃśena: 'a property of the subject, [pervaded] by a part of that', not 'a part of the subject quality'.

note: Tracks the vyāpti discussion reasonably but swaps pervader and pervaded at a point where the argument turns on them.
A faithful rendering of the body-consciousness argument, with the root-text lemmata correctly identified.

errors.english: thoroughly understands what the causes and conditions of transformation are
errors.why: འགྱུར་བ completes the previous side's སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་དག་པར་: the causes and conditions by which beings become purified, not of 'transformation'.

fix.find: thoroughly understands what the causes and conditions of transformation are
fix.replace: thoroughly understands what the causes and conditions are by which beings become purified

errors.english: and the entry is shown as meditative absorption
errors.why: སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ is samāpatti (meditative attainment), paired with samādhi, not 'entry'.

note: Good sūtra rendering with the dependent-origination and samādhi vocabulary handled well, apart from the opening clause and samāpatti.

errors.why: The phrase continues on the next side as an instrumental ('by the very meditation, as taught, endowed with scripture and reasoning'); it does not introduce a quotation.

note: A faithful rendering of the Akṣayamati quotation and the gradual-path argument.
